title: Kernel entropy bench: INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ scenario sweep
content:
Summary:

Quick working notes for a narrow, exploratory benchmark focused on how per-kernel entropy (loosely: activation/value distribution complexity) interacts with various quantization pipelines and kernel implementations. The hypothesis we want to check: kernels with adaptive per-tile handling (branching on measured entropy) can preserve more quality at tight quant budgets (INT8/AWQ) without large throughput regressions, compared to static packing kernels. This is a follow-up to the November 2026 stability sweep but with a focus on input distribution heterogeneity and small-batch worst-path behavior.

Why this experiment:
- Multiple customer incidents have highlighted that heavy tail prompts (long instructions + code) trigger worse quality regressions under AWQ/GPTQ even when average-case tests look fine (see JIRA-RT-4127).
- We need an efficient way to detect these worst-path distributions in CI and produce a per-model kernel recommendation for production routing policies.
- Prior quant benches focused on average perplexity / ROUGE. This doc captures a per-prompt distributional sweep and kernel-level profiling traces to find opportunities for adaptive fallback.

Experiment goals:
1) Measure quality delta (token-level log-prob and top-1 mismatch) and perf (p95 latency, mean throughput) across four quant pipelines: INT8 symmetric, FP8 (E4M3-like sim), GPTQ (8/4 pruning-enabled), and AWQ (per-layer adaptive).
2) Compare three kernel families: static packed kernels (v2-pack), vectorized microkernels (v3-lane), and entropy-aware tiled kernels (prototype: v4-entropy).
3) Understand small-batch (b=1..4) spikes vs batched (b=16..64) behavior to model worst-path SLO risk.
4) Produce a lightweight decision heuristic for runtime routing: when to fallback to a higher-precision kernel/model.

Hardware & infra:
- Node: g5.2x / 1x H100-80GB equivalent (internal emulation with GPU config pinned).
- Serving image: rwinf/serving-runtime:bench-20270420 (includes debug tracing hooks).
- Host: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.3, cuBLAS/cuDNN pinned to the bench image.
- Measurement harness: bench-client v0.22 (replay harness that replays exact prompt traces and collects token-level probabilities).

Models tested:
- small: Llama2-7B (fp32 baseline)
- medium: Mixtral-8x7B-like (quantization-sensitive architecture)
- large-ish: CodeCompanion-13B (instruction+code heavy; shows long-tail tokens)

Dataset / prompts:
- Base corpus: 3k prompt mixes sampled from internal prompt corpora (support chat, code completion, summarization, math).
- Tail-heavy subset (200 prompts): long instruction + code blocks, nested bullet lists, and payloads with many rare tokens (emojis, long identifiers).
- Synthetic high-entropy inputs: procedural noise prompts where token distribution is intentionally flat to stress quantization.

Measurement methodology:
- For each (model, quant-pipeline, kernel), run 3 seeds of the 3k corpus at batch sizes [1,2,4,8,16,32]. Record per-prompt token-level log-probs, top-k distribution shifts, p95/p99 latency, and memory consumption (GPU peak).
- For the tail-heavy subset, run additional high-resolution traces capturing internal kernel timers (tile-level) and activation histograms per-layer.
- Compute two primary quality metrics: average token negative log-likelihood (NLL) delta vs fp32 baseline, and Top-1 token mismatch rate on next-token prediction.
- Compute perf delta: p95 latency ratio vs baseline kernel, throughput per GPU.

Preliminary findings (high level):
- Across models, INT8 symmetric + v2-pack kernels give the best throughput but show the largest quality variance on the tail-heavy subset: median NLL delta is ~0.12 but 95th-percentile delta climbs to 0.9 on CodeCompanion-13B for certain prompts.
- AWQ pipelines (with per-layer adaptation) reduce 95th-percentile NLL delta by ~30% relative to naive INT8 for the tail subset, but throughput drops vary by kernel: v3-lane suffers 15-20% throughput loss, while v4-entropy recovers most of the throughput (5-8% loss) because it avoids unnecessary higher-precision handling for low-entropy tiles.
- FP8 (simulated E4M3) sits in the middle: consistent quality (NLL delta ~0.05 median, 95p ~0.25), with modest throughput drop (10-12%) on vectorized kernels.
- GPTQ results vary heavily with the pruning hyperparameters; aggressive pruning + v2-pack causes severe p95 latency spikes due to cache miss amplification in the microkernel scheduler.

Micro-observations (tile-level):
- For CodeCompanion-13B, layers 24-30 show the worst entropy spikes (long variable names + bracket nesting). In v2-pack these tiles are packed aggressively and cause dequantization loops to diverge, increasing per-token compute and memory stalls.
- v4-entropy kernel adds a cheap per-tile pre-pass (approx 120ns/tile) computing a small sketch (histogram sketch) and routes high-entropy tiles to a mixed-precision microkernel. This pre-pass cost is amortized for batched workloads and pays back for b<=4 where it prevents repeated costly fallback later.
- Vector lanes (v3-lane) are sensitive to alignment; misaligned tail sequences (non-power-of-two token spans) cause lane masking overheads that show as jitter in p99 for batch sizes 8-16.

Quality tradeoff examples (selected):
- Prompt A (code-heavy): fp32 logprob baseline -4.1; INT8+v2-pack -> -6.0 (NLL delta 1.9); AWQ+v4-entropy -> -4.35 (delta 0.25)
- Prompt B (long instruction): fp32 -2.9; FP8+v3-lane -> -3.05 (delta 0.15) with p95 latency +11%

Operational implications:
- For hosted API tiers with strict p95 SLOs, AWQ+v4-entropy looks promising as a default for few workloads: it gives a strong worst-path bound with only small throughput loss.
- For dedicated throughput-oriented pools where customers accept occasional quality dips, INT8+v2-pack remains attractive for batched workloads b>=16.
- We should add prompt-level entropy heuristics into our routing layer: compute a cheap sketch client-side (or at edge) and tag requests for "entropy-risk" to preferentially route to mixed-precision or AWQ variants. This reduces runtime overhead compared to broad conservative fallbacks.

Next experiments (short list):
1) Full CI run with 10k prompt corpus and more seeds to stabilize statistical claims.
2) Instrumented run on our private infra (on-prem H100 cluster) to validate cache/memory interaction differences.
3) Cost modeling: compute token-level CPU/GPU cost delta and translate to $/1M tokens for each pipeline.
4) Small A/B test: expose AWQ+v4-entropy to 5% of real traffic for telemetry on customer-facing prompts (requires feature gating + opt-in).

Immediate action items:
- (Priya) Hook bench-client to output per-prompt entropy sketch and store along with trace outputs (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/bench-client/pull/57).
- (Liam) Stabilize v4-entropy per-tile sketch implementation; reduce false positives on high-frequency tokens (ticket: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/issues/2032).
- (Marco) Draft routing heuristic RFC for product-team review: include client-side sketch, server routing policy, and fallback cost budget. Link RFC to CONFLUENCE-RT/entropy-quant-playbook.

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self style):
- How much does tokenizer choice influence measured entropy? Should we normalize sketches by subtokenization frequency?
- Is a 120ns pre-pass sustainable in edge devices (VPC private deployments) or only for hosted/dedicated? Add device-specific thresholds.
- Need a way to surface these per-prompt quality regressions into Redwood Optimize so solutions engines can recommend kernel/model combos automatically.

Appendix: quick notes on measurement noise and caveats
- Bench harness currently doesn't fully emulate multi-tenant noise; some p99 jitter may be higher in prod.
- We used simulated FP8; hardware FP8 math paths might differ (rounding, saturation).
- GPTQ pruning variant used here was intermediate; recommend repeating with the latest pruning hyperparameters from research (see PR#1983).

If you're reading this and want to run a selective repro: ping me in #eng-quant-kernels and I will share a runbook and a workspace with the bench traces.

-- Priya
